content: The document titled Guidelines on the Public Health Response to Pretreatment HIV Drug Resistance was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in July 2017. It provides detailed recommendations for addressing pretreatment HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) in individuals initiating or reinitiating first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART). This includes those who have never been exposed to antiretroviral (ARV) drugs and those with prior ARV exposure. HIV drug resistance occurs due to genetic mutations in the HIV virus, which reduce the effectiveness of specific drugs or drug combinations in suppressing viral replication. All current antiretroviral drugs, including newer drug classes, are susceptible to partial or complete inactivation due to the emergence of drug-resistant HIV strains. HIVDR is categorized into three main types: 1. Acquired HIVDR: This develops when mutations arise during viral replication in individuals receiving ARV drugs. 2. Transmitted HIVDR: This is detected in ARV drug-naïve individuals who have no history of ARV exposure but are infected with a drug-resistant strain of the virus. 3. Pretreatment HIVDR: This is identified in individuals initiating ART for the first time or reinitiating ART after prior ARV exposure. It can result from either transmitted or acquired HIVDR, or both. The guidelines emphasize the importance of addressing pretreatment HIVDR, particularly resistance to non-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), as it can compromise the success of HIV treatment programs and hinder global efforts to end the AIDS epidemic. The document outlines specific public health actions triggered when the prevalence of pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs exceeds a defined threshold. The publication supplements Chapter 4 of the 2016 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on the Use of Antiretroviral Drugs for Treating and Preventing HIV Infection. It provides evidence-based strategies to support countries in mitigating the impact of pretreatment HIVDR and achieving global HIV treatment targets. The document also includes definitions for age groups to guide the implementation of recommendations: Adults: Individuals older than 19 years. Adolescents: Individuals aged 10 to 19 years. Children: Individuals aged 1 to younger than 10 years. Infants: Children younger than 1 year. The guidelines were developed with contributions from a diverse group of experts, including clinicians, researchers, and public health professionals from various countries and institutions. The development process involved systematic reviews, modeling studies, and consultations with stakeholders to ensure the recommendations are robust and applicable across different settings. The WHO acknowledges the contributions of numerous individuals and organizations in the development of these guidelines. Special thanks are extended to the Guideline Development Group, systematic review teams, external reviewers, and WHO staff who provided technical, administrative, and editorial support. The publication underscores the importance of adhering to licensing terms for reuse and adaptation of the content. It also includes disclaimers clarifying that the views expressed do not necessarily reflect the official position of WHO regarding the legal status of countries, territories, or boundaries. Additionally, the mention of specific companies or products does not imply endorsement by WHO. In summary, the guidelines aim to equip countries with the tools and knowledge to effectively respond to pretreatment HIVDR, thereby improving the outcomes of HIV treatment programs and advancing global efforts to combat the AIDS epidemic.
